entries.narration: This course follows a small team building a reporting dashboard for a business partner, and the first thing to settle is what we mean by a soft skill. Here it means something you do, that another person could notice: asking a question before assuming, stating a request clearly, following through on what you said, and repairing a mistake when you make one. Those are behaviours, and behaviours can be practised. It is just as important to say what a soft skill is not. It is not extroversion; some of the best listeners are quiet. It is not an accent, or one particular way of speaking. It is not being available at every hour. And it is not one culture's style presented as the only correct one. The right move also depends on context. Who has the power to decide, and who carries the risk? What happens if the message is misread? What are the team's habits, and the local norms and policies? The same words can be right in one situation and wrong in another. So this course shows reasons and options, not one perfect script. Next, how you know what you are good at.

How do you know what you are good at? Most people answer with labels: I'm a good communicator, I'm a team player, I'm bad at deadlines, I'm too quiet. Labels are hard to act on, and easy for someone else to dispute. Evidence works better. Take Sam, the analyst on the dashboard project, two weeks in. Good communicator becomes: Sam summarised the brief back to Priya, the business partner, and Priya corrected one point before any work began. Bad at deadlines becomes: Sam missed the draft due on the fourth, and said so on the fifth. Too quiet becomes: Sam raised the data risk in writing rather than in the meeting. Each one names a situation, what Sam did, and what happened next. Now read the evidence. A strength is a behaviour that worked more than once: checking understanding early. A development need is a specific behaviour to change, not a flaw in character: flagging a slipping date sooner. Some patterns are about context: Sam contributes best in writing, which is useful to know rather than something to fix. Then pick one small next step. Next, separating what happened from what we make of it.

Late on a Tuesday afternoon, Priya sends Sam a message: can the dashboard split sales by region for Thursday's demo? Sam reads it and, within a second, several things happen at once. It helps to pull them apart. The observation is plain: a new request, two days before the demo. The interpretation arrives just as fast: Priya ignores our plan. That is a guess about Priya's motive, and it feels like a fact. Then the feeling: frustration, and some anxiety about Thursday. The feeling is real and worth noticing; it is not something to suppress. And finally the action, the reply Sam sends. When these blur together, the guess drives the reply. A simple test helps. Could a camera record it? Then it is an observation. If not, it is an interpretation, which is a hypothesis that can be checked. Then name what is unknown. Here, Sam does not know why Priya is asking, or what changed. Acting on the observation and the open question, rather than on the guess, leaves far more good options open. Next, what to do with the feeling.

Some situations reliably produce a strong reaction. For Sam, a late change request while already behind on the export is one of them. Call it a trigger. You cannot always prevent the reaction, and you do not need to. What you can usually choose is what you do next. The body often notices first: a tight jaw, typing faster than usual. That is the moment for a pause, even a short one: write the reply, then wait ten minutes before sending. Regulating emotion in this sense is a choice about behaviour, not about hiding or denying a feeling. Now compare three replies. Sam could agree resentfully: fine, whatever you need. The work grows, Sam works late in silence, and nobody discusses the trade-off. Sam could push back hard: that's not how this works. Priya learns to share changes later, not sooner, which makes the next surprise worse. Or Sam could pause and ask what changed, promising options. That brings out the real reason. Notice that the third reply is not agreement. It is deciding with information. And it is about Sam's behaviour, never a diagnosis of Priya's. Next, seeing Priya's side.

Sam's interpretation was that Priya changes plans on a whim. Perspective-taking means considering how the same situation looks from Priya's position, and then checking, rather than replacing one assumption with another. So Sam asked: what's behind the change, and who will be there? The answer changed the picture. Priya's director had moved the review forward. Regional leads would now attend, so a regional view suddenly mattered. And one region breakdown was enough; Priya did not need the whole dashboard rebuilt. None of that was visible in the original message. Two limits keep this kind of empathy useful. First, ask about the situation, not about the person's character or feelings; do not guess at someone's state of mind, and certainly do not diagnose it. Let them tell you. Second, understanding someone's reasons is not the same as agreeing to everything. Sam now understands the request, and still has to decide what is possible by Thursday. It is also worth remembering that role, culture and language all shape how a request is phrased, so a short message is not necessarily a careless one. Next, saying what you can and cannot do.

With the reason understood, Sam still has to answer, and this is where assertiveness comes in. Assertiveness means stating your view, your limits and your options clearly, while respecting the other person's. It sits between two easier extremes. A passive reply, sure, no problem, avoids the conversation, but hides the fact that the export will slip, which Priya will discover later. An aggressive reply, you always do this, protects Sam's time but ignores Priya's reason, and damages the relationship. The assertive reply has four parts. Acknowledge what matters: the region view matters for the demo. State the limit plainly: I can't deliver it and the export by Thursday. Offer real options: regions Thursday and the export Monday, or both on Monday. And ask who decides, while keeping Alex, the team lead, informed. That is a boundary with options, not a wall. Integrity sits underneath it: never promise what you cannot deliver, even when promising is easier. And confidence, in this sense, is clarity about what you know and do not know, not certainty about everything. Next chapter: listening.

Chapter two is about listening, and it starts with a sentence from Priya: the dashboard has to be real time. There are two ways to hear that. One is listening to reply. Sam already knows what real time usually means to an analyst, so Sam answers before Priya has finished: sure, we can stream it. That sounds helpful. It is also a promise built on a guess, and it commits the team to something expensive that Priya may not need. The other is listening to understand, which means holding the answer back until you know what the other person is trying to achieve. Sam asks: real time for which decision? That question costs nothing, and it is the one that finds out what is really needed. A few habits make that kind of attention visible. Let the other person finish. Take notes in their words, rather than writing your counter-arguments. Keep to one screen instead of answering chat on the side. And interrupt only to check a word you did not follow. Attention can look different for different people; what matters is its effect. Next, the questions themselves.

Once Sam decides to ask rather than promise, the next question is which questions to ask. Different kinds get different things. An open question, such as what will you use it for, invites Priya to describe the purpose in Priya's own terms. A focused question, how old can the numbers be, pins down a limit. A probing question, what happens if they are two hours old, finds what is actually at stake, which is often where the real requirement hides. A closed question, is noon early enough, is useful at the end, when you want a clear yes or no. And a leading question, daily is fine, right, is the one to avoid, because it tends to get your own answer handed back to you, especially when there is a difference in power. A sequence that works most of the time is to start open, so the other person sets the frame; then focus on numbers, dates and limits; probe anything that surprises you; and close by confirming one decision. It is a sequence, not a script, and a good conversation will loop back. Next, checking that you understood.

After the questions, Sam checks understanding by saying it back. There are two related moves. Paraphrasing says one point back in your own words. Summarising gathers several points and puts them in order. Sam's summary does both: what I heard is that store managers check stock levels; the decision is whether to reorder before noon; and the limit is that numbers from this morning are enough. Then comes the most useful sentence in the summary: what have I got wrong? Priya corrects one detail. Not once a day: two updates, at six and at eleven. That correction is the point. A summary that never draws a correction may simply not have been listened to. Saying it back in your own words shows understanding, while repeating someone's exact words only shows memory. And the way you ask matters. Is that right invites a polite yes, especially from someone who does not want to seem difficult. What have I got wrong invites the correction you actually need, and makes it easy to give. Next, what is underneath a request.

Underneath most requests there are three layers, and it helps to separate them. The request is what someone asks for, in their words: real-time numbers on the dashboard. The need is what it is for. Here, store managers want to spot low stock before the noon reorder, in every region. And the constraints are what limit the possible answers: the source data loads every two hours, there is no budget for streaming, and the data feed belongs to Jordan, the data engineer. Once the layers are separate, better options appear. Two loads a day, at six and eleven, meet the need. A low-stock flag that highlights what to reorder may meet it even better than fresher numbers. And Sam can ask Jordan whether the eleven o'clock load could move earlier. Notice the option that does not appear: streaming. It matches the words of the request, real time, but not the need, and it breaks a constraint. Sam's job is not to choose for Priya, but to bring options that fit to the person who owns the decision. Next, listening across different backgrounds.

Listening gets harder when people come from different backgrounds, and that includes professional backgrounds. When Priya says real time, Priya means this morning's numbers. When Jordan, the data engineer, hears real time, Jordan hears within seconds. Refresh means the page updating to one, and a pipeline run to the other. Region is a sales area in one conversation and a cloud data centre in the next. Nobody is wrong; the same word belongs to different fields. Language background adds another layer. Someone working in their second or third language may follow perfectly well but need a moment longer, or find a written version easier than fast speech. A few habits help everyone. Define key words out loud: by real time, I mean numbers no older than this morning. Prefer plain words to idioms and acronyms. Follow a conversation with a short written summary that people can reread at their own pace. Allow time to process before expecting an answer. And check understanding without turning it into a test of the other person. Next, the signals that are easy to misread.

After Sam's summary, Priya goes quiet. It is tempting to read that silence as agreement and move on. But silence, like most cues, has several possible meanings. It might be agreement, with nothing to add. It might be uncertainty, not knowing what to ask. It might simply be thinking time. Or it might be a doubt that Priya has decided not to voice, perhaps because the meeting is running late. The same goes for other cues. Norms around eye contact differ between cultures and between individuals, including many neurodivergent people, so less eye contact does not mean less attention. A camera can be off for any number of ordinary reasons. A nod can mean I follow you rather than I agree. None of these cues has one universal meaning, so treat a cue as a reason to ask, not as an answer. Sam can ask directly: what would you change? And offer another channel: if it is easier, reply in writing later. That turns a guess about a silence into actual information. Next, closing the conversation well.

The last move in a good conversation is closing it, so that everyone leaves with the same understanding. Sam's closing recap has four parts. What was decided: two loads a day, at six and eleven. What is still open: whether the eleven o'clock load can move earlier, which is Jordan's to answer. What the team is not doing: streaming, for now. Saying that out loud matters, because things nobody rejected explicitly have a way of quietly coming back as expectations. And an invitation to correct: reply by Thursday if anything is wrong. Then the next steps. Each action has one named owner and a date: Jordan checks the load time by Wednesday, Sam drafts the low-stock flag rules by Thursday, Priya confirms the demo regions by Thursday. Owners agree to their own actions; nobody is volunteered in their absence. And the recap goes out in writing the same day, because a spoken recap fades by Friday. Understanding the message is the first half of communication. The next chapter is about expressing it clearly to the next audience.

Chapter three is about speaking clearly, and clarity starts before you open your mouth. Here is the fact: the eleven o'clock data load ran three hours late. That one fact needs a different message for each person who should hear it. Jordan, the data engineer, needs to fix it, so the main point for Jordan is that the job failed twice and why. Alex, the team lead, needs to adjust the plan, so the main point is that Thursday's demo is at risk. Priya needs to decide what to show at the demo, so the main point is that the regional numbers may be stale. Same fact, three main points. Four questions help before speaking. What is the purpose: to inform, to ask for something, or to get a decision? Who is the audience, and what do they already know? What is the context: what else is on their mind today? And what is the main point, in a single sentence? If you cannot yet say the main point in one sentence, you are probably not ready to say it to someone else. Next, organising what comes after the point.

Once the main point is clear, the next question is order. Most of us explain things in story order, the order they happened to us. So on Monday, Jordan noticed the load was late, and then the retry failed, and later it turned out, which meant that, and finally, so Thursday is at risk. The listener spends the whole explanation not knowing what to listen for, and the point, when it arrives, arrives just as their attention drifts. Turn it round. Put the point first: Thursday's demo is at risk. Then the reasons, two or three at most: the load failed twice, and the fix needs Jordan until Wednesday. Then the ask, if there is one: can we decide today? Detail, such as which job failed and how the retry behaved, comes when someone asks for it, and Alex may not need it at all. Point first can feel abrupt the first few times. In practice it is a courtesy: it tells people why they are listening, and lets them stop you when they have heard enough. Next, explaining technical ideas to people outside the field.

Explaining a technical problem to someone outside the field is a skill of its own. For engineers, Jordan would say the ingest job hit a lock timeout. That is precise, and almost meaningless to Priya. For Priya, Sam says the morning data arrived three hours late. Both are true; each fits its audience. Plain language starts from the effect on the listener, not from the mechanism. Analogies help, but they need limits. The data feed is like a delivery that comes twice a day, which explains why the numbers are a few hours old. But unlike a delivery, paying more cannot make it come faster, because the delay is in the source system. If Sam leaves that limit unsaid, Priya may reasonably ask why the team does not just pay for an express service. Say where an analogy breaks before someone relies on it. A few checks keep a plain explanation honest. Lead with the effect. Define one term at most, and only if it is needed. Describe what happened, not who to blame. And ask whether it made sense, then actually listen to the answer. Next, making requests.

A request in a group chat that says can someone look at the feed asks everyone, which in practice means it asks no one. Everyone assumes someone else will pick it up. A specific request has four parts. Who: Jordan, could you. What: move the eleven o'clock load to ten. Why: so the stores see the numbers before the noon reorder. And by when: by Wednesday, if possible. The why is easy to leave out, and it matters, because it lets Jordan suggest a better way to meet the same need, perhaps one Sam had not thought of. Then check agreement, and listen carefully to the answer. Jordan says: probably, I'll confirm by three. That is useful, and it is not yet a yes. Sam notes it as pending rather than reporting it to Priya as done. Make it easy to say no or to propose another date, because a request that cannot be refused is really an instruction, and people respond to instructions differently. Thank people for an answer, whatever it is. And when the answer arrives, confirm it in writing. Next, what to say when you do not know.

Priya asks the question everyone asks: will it be fixed by Thursday? Sam does not know. There are several ways to answer. Definitely, no problem, sounds reassuring, and claims a certainty Sam does not have; if Thursday slips, Priya will remember the definitely. No idea is honest, but leaves Priya with nothing to plan around. I don't know yet, I'll know by three, is honest and gives a next step. And likely, if Jordan's fix holds, states the condition the answer depends on, which is exactly what Priya needs to judge the risk. Saying I don't know yet is not a weakness; it is accurate, and it is what makes your later certainty believable. Asking for help is the other half of this. A good request for help says what you tried, so the helper does not repeat it: Sam reran the job and read the log. It says where you are stuck: the lock is in another team's system. It says what you need: ten minutes with Jordan. And by when: before the three o'clock update. Asking early is almost always cheaper than being rescued late. Next, saying no.

Here is a harder moment. Alex, the team lead, asks Sam to tell Priya everything will be ready on Thursday. Sam cannot honestly promise that. There are three broad ways to answer. Sam could give in: OK, I'll tell Priya. That avoids an awkward minute now, and creates a promise nobody can keep. Sam could snap: that's unrealistic and you know it. That might be true, but Alex is now defending the date instead of looking at the risk. Or Sam could be firm: I can't promise all of it, and here are two options. The firm answer has a structure. The concern, stated as fact: the region view depends on Jordan's fix on Wednesday. The options: show the regions on Thursday with a clear caveat, or show them on Monday. Who decides: Alex and Priya choose, and Sam does not make a commitment on their behalf. And the record: once they choose, Sam writes it down. Respectful disagreement can stay firm. Confidence here is not certainty about everything; it is being clear about what is known and what is not. Next chapter: writing.

Chapter four turns to writing, and the first decision is not what to write but where. The same message lands very differently in a conversation, a chat message, an email or a document. A conversation, in person or on a call, is best for tension, nuance and fast back-and-forth, but it leaves no record. Chat is good for quick questions and short updates, and poor for decisions that people will need to find a month later. Email suits one clear request, often to someone outside the team. And a document is the place for decisions, plans and handovers that people will look up. A few rules of thumb follow. Talk, then write: discuss something live, then send a short written summary of what was agreed. Move tension out of chat; a disagreement that is going badly in writing usually goes better in a five-minute call. If anyone will need to find it later, write it somewhere durable. If it is urgent, call, because an email can sit unread for hours. And check your team's own norms, because they often differ. Next, the structure of a message.

A busy reader decides from the subject line and the first sentence whether a message needs them now. So put the request and the deadline where they will be seen. Look at Sam's email to Priya, one part at a time. The subject says what it is and when: demo, region decision by Wednesday noon. The opening says what is needed, in one sentence: I need one decision from you. Then the context, kept short: the region data may be three hours late on Thursday. Then the request itself, as a clear choice: show the regions with a note, or wait until Monday? Then the deadline. And a close that offers another channel: happy to talk if that's easier. Notice what is not there: the history of the data feed, or a paragraph of apology. Tone is the other half. Writing loses the voice, so a written message often reads harsher than the writer meant. Need this by Wednesday can sound like an order. Could you let me know by Wednesday asks for exactly the same thing. Before sending, read the message once as the recipient would. Next, status updates.

Still working on it, should be fine, is the most common status update there is, and it tells the reader nothing they can act on. A status update exists so that someone can decide something: whether to worry, whether to step in, whether to change a plan. Here is Sam's Tuesday update, rewritten. Done: the region view is built and tested. Evidence: its totals match the finance team's figures, which is what makes done believable. Blocked: the fix to the eleven o'clock load, which sits with Jordan. Risk: on Thursday the regional numbers may be three hours stale. Decision needed: Priya, should we show them with a note? And next: the export, by Friday. Every line is something the reader can use. A few habits make this routine. Separate what is done from what is planned; mixing them is how surprises happen. Name a blocker's owner plainly, without blame, so the reader knows whom to ask. And raise risks early, while there are still options, rather than on the day they turn into problems. Next, notes and decision records.

The decision about the demo regions was made the way many decisions are: forty-three chat messages, over two days, in two threads. Some of it was explicit. Some of it was a thumbs up that might have meant yes, or might have meant I saw this. And Mei, who joined the team the following week, has no way to reconstruct any of it. Decisions made in chat get scattered, stay implicit, and are lost to anyone who arrives later. A short decision record fixes that. It says what was decided: show the regions on Thursday, marked as of eleven o'clock. Who decided, and when: Priya, with Alex, on Wednesday at noon. Which options were considered: show with a note, or wait until Monday. Why this one was chosen: the regional leads need the view, and the note covers the delay honestly. And when to revisit it: if the eleven o'clock load fails again. It takes five minutes to write, and it is the document that answers the question why did we do it this way, months later. Meeting notes work the same way. Next, working across time zones.

The dashboard team is spread across time zones. Priya is in London, Jordan in Toronto, and Mei, who joined recently, in Singapore. When Sam sends a message at four in the afternoon London time, Priya and Jordan see it straight away. For Mei it arrives at midnight, and Mei will see it in the morning. That is how it should be. Nobody should feel they have to answer at midnight because a message arrived. What makes this work is agreed response expectations, matched to urgency. Something urgent gets a phone call, because a chat message can easily sit unread. Something needed today gets a chat message with a clear ask. Something for this week goes in an email or a document. And something purely for information says so: no reply needed. With those expectations agreed, a quiet colleague is just a colleague who is asleep, not someone ignoring you. One more habit makes asynchronous work much smoother: write so that the reader can act without needing to ask a follow-up question, because each question can cost a whole day across time zones. Next, checking before you send.

A written message, once sent, can be forwarded, searched and kept for years. That is its strength, and the reason for a short check before sending. Here is a near miss. To save time, Sam was about to forward a whole thread to Priya. Scrolling down, Sam noticed two things. The thread included the names of store staff, copied from data logs, which Priya had no need to see. And it contained an internal comment: Priya keeps changing it. Neither belonged in the message. Six checks catch most problems like this. Recipients: who needs this, and who does not; reply-all is rarely the answer. Sensitive information: remove personal or private detail that the reader does not need. Accessibility: use headings, give images alternative text, and prefer plain words, so the message works for screen readers and for people reading in a second language. Tone: read it once as the recipient would. Length: cut what the reader will not use. And put the request near the top, where it will be seen. These take a minute, and they protect other people as well as you. Next chapter: teamwork.

Chapter five is about teamwork, and it starts with a gap. Two weeks before the demo, nobody had decided the format of the data export. Sam assumed Jordan would set it, because Jordan owns the data. Jordan assumed Sam would decide it, because Sam builds the dashboard. Neither was being careless. Each made a reasonable assumption, and nobody had said who owned it. Teams rarely fail for lack of effort; more often, a piece of work falls between two people. A simple ownership table closes the gap. Jordan owns the data feed and its loads. Sam owns the dashboard and the export. Priya decides what the export contains, with input from finance. Alex owns the plan and priorities. And each row says what it depends on. Alongside ownership, the team agrees a few working habits: updates every Tuesday in the shared document, blockers raised the same day they appear, decisions written in the decision record, and reviews answered within one working day. These are agreements, not laws. When the work or the team changes, they are worth revisiting. Next, trust.

Trust in a team is built mostly in small moments. A promise kept, again and again, gets noticed. So does honesty: saying early that a date will slip builds trust, even though it is bad news, because people learn they will not be surprised. A missed handover costs some trust. And hiding a problem costs the most of all, because once it surfaces, people start to wonder what else they have not been told. Everyone breaks a promise sometimes. What matters then is the repair, and a good repair has four parts. Here is Sam, who missed a ten o'clock handover with Mei. Name it plainly: I missed our ten o'clock handover. State the impact on the other person: you waited a day for access. Show the fix: the access is done, and the notes are attached. And say what changes next time: handovers are now in my calendar. Notice what is not there: a long apology, or a list of reasons before the facts. Reasons can come later if they help. The repair is about the other person's experience, not about defending yourself. Next, making it safe to speak up.

Psychological safety means people can raise a concern, admit a mistake or ask a question without being punished or embarrassed for it. In Mei's first week, Mei notices that the regional totals do not match the finance figures, and says so in the team meeting. Alex could respond in two ways. Shut it down: we covered that before you joined. The topic closes, and Mei learns that questions from a newcomer are not welcome. Mei stops raising issues. Or open it up: good catch, show us where. It turns out Mei has found a real bug in how refunds are counted, weeks before the demo. Safety is not the same as comfort, and it does not replace accountability. One useful model puts the two side by side. A team with high safety and high accountability learns and improves. High safety with low accountability is comfortable, and may coast. Low safety with high accountability is anxious, and tends to hide errors. Treat the grid as one lens, not a law. Those with more power usually have to show safety first, by asking real questions and admitting their own mistakes. Next, widening who takes part.

A meeting that runs on whoever speaks first ends up hearing some people far more than others. Fast talkers, especially those speaking their first language. Senior people, to whom others tend to defer. People in the room, while remote colleagues wait for a gap that never comes. And not Mei at all, when the meeting is at one in the morning Singapore time. None of this needs anyone to be rude; it is just how the default works. Small changes to the format widen who takes part, without asking anyone to change who they are. Send the agenda a day ahead, including the questions to be decided, so people who think before they speak can prepare. Collect written input before the discussion, so the first idea in the room is not automatically the one that wins. Use a round, going to each person in turn, where anyone may pass. Turn on captions, and keep a shared document as you go, which helps people with hearing differences, people in a second language, and anyone whose connection drops. Rotate meeting times, so the late slot is shared. And pause before deciding. Next, the meeting itself.

A useful meeting is built around a question. Here the question is: do we show the regional view at Thursday's demo, yes or no? That single line changes everything else. It decides who needs to be there: only those who make the decision or have information it needs, which here is Priya, Alex, Sam and Jordan. It decides the pre-read: one page of status and risks, sent a day ahead, so the meeting does not spend twenty minutes reading aloud. And it suggests a timebox: ten minutes for facts, fifteen for options, and five to decide. Facilitating then means keeping to that shape, and noticing when the conversation drifts into a different question that deserves its own meeting. The meeting ends with a record. The decision: go, with a note saying the numbers are as of eleven o'clock. The actions, each with one owner and a date. What was parked: streaming, to revisit next quarter, written down so it does not quietly reappear. And, just as useful, what is no longer needed: the follow-up meeting on Friday can be cancelled. Next, sharing knowledge and credit.

Two habits make a team stronger over time. The first is sharing knowledge. The question how is the region total calculated was asked five times in chat over three weeks, each time answered slightly differently. A one-page note, linked from the dashboard, answers it once, and writing it down has a side effect: it exposes what nobody actually knew. Asking for help early belongs here too; it is a way of sharing the problem before it grows. The second habit is recognising contributions. Thanks, team, is kind, and forgettable. Specific recognition names who did what, and why it mattered: Jordan's fix on Wednesday is the reason the demo could show regional numbers at all. Specific recognition is more believable, and it tells everyone what the team values. Notice quiet work in particular. Mei's discovery of the refund bug did not look dramatic, but it prevented a much worse problem later. And give recognition where it counts, for example in the update Priya reads, not only in a private message. Credit the person who did the work, not only the person who presented it. Next, handovers.

Teams change. People join, leave, go on holiday or move to other projects, and every change is a moment when knowledge can be lost. When Mei joined the dashboard team, the handover note made the difference between a confusing first week and a useful one. It gave the context: what the dashboard is for, and who relies on it. It linked to the decision records, so Mei did not have to reconstruct them from chat. It listed what was still open: the eleven o'clock load and the export format. It said who to ask about what: Jordan for the data feed, Priya for scope. It made sure Mei's access was granted and tested on the first day, not discovered missing on the third. And it gave Mei a first task that was small, real and reviewed. A change in membership is also a good moment to revisit the team's agreements. Who owns what now? Do meeting times still work, with someone in Singapore? And what norms has the team been assuming, that a newcomer cannot see? Team-development models can be useful lenses here, but teams do not move through stages in a fixed order. Next chapter: ownership and priorities.

Chapter six is about commitments: making them, tracking them and changing them honestly. It starts with four words that are often blurred. Ownership means you drive a piece of work to done. Authority means you are allowed to decide it. Accountability means you answer for the outcome. And a dependency is something you need from someone else. Applied to the export: Sam owns it, and drives it to done. Priya has the authority to decide what it contains. Alex is accountable for the overall plan. And the export depends on Jordan's data feed. Separating the words makes Sam's job clearer. Owning the export means driving it, with a clear next step every week. It means flagging it, saying so as soon as the feed slips, rather than hoping. It does not mean taking the blame for other people's delays, and it does not mean deciding things that are Priya's to decide. Ownership includes communicating a dependency honestly, even when that feels like making excuses. It is the opposite of hiding it. Next, choosing what to do first.

A priority is a choice, and it should have reasons. Four reasons cover most choices: impact, how much it matters; urgency, how soon it is needed; risk, how likely it is to go wrong if left; and dependency, what else is waiting on it. Here is Sam's list on Monday. The note for the demo is high impact, due Thursday, and low risk: first. The export columns are high impact and high risk, and finance is waiting on them: second. The refund bug is high impact and high risk, and the totals depend on it: third. And the chart colours are low impact, with nothing waiting: later. Then, on Tuesday, Priya writes that finance needs the export by Friday as well. The tempting response is to say yes and add it to the pile. But adding something always means something else gives way, and the choice is what. Sam brings three options to Alex, who owns the priorities: reduce the scope with fewer columns first; move a date, so the bug fix waits a week; or add capacity, with Mei taking the polish. Whatever moves is written down, so nobody is surprised later. Next, breaking work into steps.

Do the export is on Sam's list, and it has been there for a week. That is a common pattern: a task written as a wish, too big and too vague to start. Breaking it down helps in two ways. First, milestones that other people can see. Agree the columns with Priya on Tuesday. Send a sample file to finance on Wednesday. Build from the sample on Thursday. Check the totals against finance's figures on Friday. Each milestone is a point where someone else can see progress, or see that it has stopped, without needing a meeting. Second, one concrete next action: email Priya three column options, today, thirty minutes, before eleven o'clock. A good next action starts with a verb and fits in a single sitting. It is small enough that there is no reason to put it off. And a useful check follows from this: if a milestone has no next action written against it, it is probably stuck, and it is better to notice that on Tuesday than on Friday. Next, how much fits in a week.

A plan that assumes Sam has thirty-seven uninterrupted hours this week will fail, because nobody has that week. A realistic plan starts from actual capacity. Sam's contract is thirty-seven hours. About eight go to meetings. About four go to answering support questions about the existing reports. About five more disappear into interruptions and the cost of switching between tasks. That leaves roughly twenty hours of focus time. The estimates are better given as ranges than as single numbers, because a single number hides uncertainty. The export will take eight to fourteen hours. The refund bug, four to twelve, because the cause is still unknown and that is where most of the uncertainty sits. The demo note, one to two. The total is thirteen to twenty-eight hours, against about twenty available. In other words, the plan may fit, or may not, and that is worth saying now, on Monday, rather than discovering on Friday. A few habits help capacity too: protect blocks of focus time, and batch questions into fewer interruptions where the team can agree to. Next, saying early when a plan will not hold.

On Tuesday morning, Sam discovers that the refund bug is bigger than expected. There is now no way to finish both the export and the fix this week. The question is when to say so. The same news has very different value at different times. On Tuesday morning, there are still options: fewer columns in the export first, a later date for the fix, or some help from Mei. On Thursday night, the only thing left is an apology. So Sam writes to Alex and Priya on Tuesday. What changed: the refund bug is bigger than we thought. The impact: the export and the bug fix will not both fit this week. The options: fewer columns first, a later fix, or extra help. And who decides, and by when: could you choose by Wednesday noon? Raising it early is not a failure. It is information, given while it is still useful, and it lets other people adjust their own plans too: finance can plan around a smaller export. Late news turns a planning problem into a trust problem, because people wonder what else they have not been told. Next, following through, including on mistakes.

Even with good planning, a commitment will sometimes be missed. The sample file for finance was due on Wednesday, and it is not ready. Sam has two broad choices. One is to hide it: say nothing, work all weekend, and hope nobody notices. That feels responsible, and usually is not. Sam ends up tired, the file is often late anyway, and when it comes out, trust is lost, because the problem was concealed. The other is to tell people: it's late, it will be ready by Friday noon, with the totals checked. Finance can then plan around the real date, which is what they needed. Following through means owning the miss: saying so, fixing it, and learning from it. It does not mean taking responsibility for everything. Other people's delays are theirs to explain. And there is a boundary worth keeping. Hidden overtime props up a plan that was never realistic, and makes the next plan just as unrealistic. When a plan cannot be met with reasonable effort, the professional move is to escalate it, not to absorb it. No personal habit fixes an unsustainable workload. Next chapter: thinking problems through together.

Chapter seven is about thinking problems through together, and it starts with framing. When the export started slipping, Alex's first reaction was: we're behind, everyone push harder. That is understandable, and it is a reaction, not a problem statement. Framing turns it into something a team can work on. The problem: the export will not be ready by Friday. The outcome actually wanted: finance can close the month on Monday. The constraints: month-end is on Monday, and there are no new people to add. And what is not the problem: the chart colours, or streaming, which keep coming up but do not affect Monday at all. The most useful line here is the outcome. Export by Friday has only one answer: work harder. Finance can close the month on Monday has several, and some of them may not need the full export at all. Constraints, meanwhile, rule options out early, before anyone spends effort on them. A good frame ends with a question: how might we give finance what it needs by Monday? And it is worth agreeing the frame before anyone starts debating solutions. Next, sorting what we know from what we assume.

A problem-solving meeting mixes several kinds of statement, often in the same breath, and they need different treatment. Here is what was said in the meeting about the export. Jordan missed two updates. That is a fact, and it can be checked in the update log. Jordan isn't trying. That is an assumption about effort, and it is quite a different claim: an observed missed update is not evidence of low effort. The only way to check it is to ask Jordan, who, it turns out, has been covering a second team's outage. The fix takes a week. That is an estimate; ask for the breakdown behind it. Finance needs every column. An assumption, and an important one, because it drives the whole scope; ask finance. The old report was better. An opinion, and a question: better in what way? Sorting the statements also shows what nobody knows yet. Which columns finance really uses. What actually causes the late loads. Naming that missing evidence before choosing an option is often the most useful thing a meeting can do. Next, generating options.

Once the problem is framed, the next temptation is to debate the first option anyone mentions. In this team, that was moving the date. Debating one option quickly becomes a yes or no argument. Generating several alternatives before judging any of them usually leads somewhere better. So the team takes five minutes to widen. Less scope: just the six columns finance actually uses. A later date: the export next Wednesday. More support: Mei helps with the build. Phased: a manual file on Monday, so finance can close, and the automated export later. Reuse: patch the old report for one more month. And one deliberately unusual option, ask finance to wait a month, which is unlikely, but shows where the edges are. Only then does the team narrow. Rule out the options that break a constraint: waiting a month misses month-end. And combine what remains, because the best answer is often a combination: less scope, delivered in phases. One practical tip: collect options in writing first, before discussing them, so the first or loudest idea does not win by default. Next, comparing the options.

With a short list of options, a weighted table can help compare them. The team agrees four criteria: whether finance can close the month on Monday, accuracy, the load on the team, and how much rework it creates later. Each criterion gets a weight, reflecting what the team values most, and each option gets a score from one to five against each criterion. Multiply and add, and the totals come out: less scope thirty-five, a later date thirty-three, phased thirty. It is tempting to read that as an answer. It is not quite one. The totals are close, so the decision is still a judgement. And the weights are preferences, not facts: someone chose to weight finance closing on Monday at three, and team load at two. Say whose preferences they are. The real value of the table is that it shows where people disagree, which is usually about a weight or a score, not about the whole option. A useful check is to swap two weights and see whether the winner changes. If it does, the decision depends on that preference, and that is what to discuss. Use the table to structure a conversation, not to end it. Next, the traps in group reasoning.

Groups reason badly in some predictable ways, and naming a trap is not enough. Each needs a small countermeasure that is built into how the meeting runs. The first trap is confirmation bias: once the team liked the phased option, it gathered evidence for it and none against it. The countermeasure is a question asked out loud: what would change our mind? It turns looking for agreement into looking for evidence. The second is premature agreement. Alex, the team lead, spoke first, and everyone agreed within a minute. That may have been genuine agreement, or it may have been deference, and there is no way to tell. The countermeasure is to have everyone write down their view before the discussion starts, so the first voice does not set the answer. The third is false certainty: phased will definitely work. The countermeasure is a pre-mortem. Imagine it is two weeks from now and the phased plan has failed, and list the reasons why. People find it easier to name risks this way than to challenge a plan directly. These work best as routine habits, used every time, so that using them never feels like an accusation. Next, matching care to the decision.

Not every decision deserves the same care, and a team that debates everything at the same length will be slow on the easy decisions and rushed on the hard ones. Two questions help: who owns the decision, and how reversible is it? The wording of the note on the demo is easily changed, and Sam can decide it today. The phased export can be undone within a week, so Alex and Priya decide it this week. Moving the data loads to ten o'clock can be reversed, but carries risk, so Jordan decides it, after a trial. Changing the data supplier would be hard to undo, and it belongs to Priya's director, over months. Where a question can be answered by trying, a small experiment often beats an argument. Instead of debating whether a ten o'clock load would be on time, Jordan proposes to try it for three days, measure how late each load is, stop early if a load fails twice, and decide on Friday. The experiment is proportionate: small, reversible and time-boxed. And it replaces opinions with evidence. Next, what happens when the evidence comes in.

A decision record is most useful at the moment you need to change your mind. The team's record says what was chosen: less scope, delivered in phases, with six columns. How: a manual file on Monday, and the export on Wednesday. Why: finance can close on Monday, and accuracy is kept. And, importantly, what it assumed: that the ten o'clock loads would be on time. Next to that assumption sits a revisit trigger: if the ten o'clock trial is late twice, look at this again. Then the evidence came in. On Tuesday the load was on time. On Wednesday it was forty minutes late. On Thursday, seventy. The assumption failed, so the trigger fired, and the team knew exactly which part of the plan to revisit, rather than reopening everything. The revised recommendation keeps the manual file for Monday, which still works, and leaves the loads at eleven o'clock. Changing a decision because the evidence changed is good reasoning, not a U-turn. It is much easier to do without loss of face when the record already said what would change it. Next chapter: feedback.

Chapter eight is about feedback: giving it, receiving it, and turning it into change. Before any words, four checks decide whether feedback can be heard at all. On Wednesday, Jordan missed a handover, and Mei waited a day for the information. Sam is annoyed. The first check is purpose. Feedback exists to help someone change something, here, to make handovers reliable. It is not a way to relieve Sam's frustration, and if venting is the real purpose, it is better to wait. The second is timing: soon, this week, but once Sam is calm. The third is privacy: one to one, not in front of the team at the stand-up. And the fourth is permission: can we talk about Wednesday's handover? Asking first lets Jordan choose a moment to listen. The opposite of each check shows why they matter. Feedback given in front of the team reads as a reprimand. Feedback sent by chat while angry carries the anger more than the issue. At five to six on a Friday, there is no time to respond. And feedback saved up for weeks arrives as an ambush. Next, what to actually say.

Sam's first draft, in the privacy of Sam's own head, was: you're unreliable. That is a judgement about a person. It is hard to act on, because it does not say what to change, and it is easy to reject, because one counter-example disproves it. The Center for Creative Leadership's model, called SBI, offers a better structure: situation, behaviour, impact. The situation: at Wednesday's ten o'clock handover. The behaviour: the load notes weren't sent. The impact: Mei waited a day, and finance's file slipped. Each part has a simple test. The situation should be specific: when and where, exactly, not generally or always. The behaviour should be something a camera could record, which rules out words like careless or unreliable. And the impact should describe an effect, on people or on the work, rather than delivering a verdict. Feedback built this way is much easier to hear, because it is about one thing that happened, and much easier to act on, because it says what mattered. SBI is an aid to having the conversation, though, not a script that guarantees a particular response. Next, the step SBI leaves out.

SBI describes what happened and its effect. The Center for Creative Leadership's extension, SBII, adds a fourth step: ask about intent. People act for reasons you cannot see from where you sit, and the reason often changes what the right fix is. So after describing the impact, Sam asks: what was going on for you on Wednesday? Jordan explains: another team had an outage, and Jordan was pulled in to help with it all morning. Sam acknowledges that: that makes sense. And keeps the impact in view: it still left Mei waiting. Jordan agrees: fair, I should have said so. Notice what the account changed and what it did not. The impact stays the same; Mei still waited a day. But the fix is different. If the cause had been carelessness, the fix might have been a reminder. Since the cause was being pulled away, the fix is a named backup for handovers and a one-line note when it happens, not try harder. Intent is asked, never assumed and never diagnosed. And context explains a behaviour; it is not a free pass. Next, the other side: receiving feedback.

Now look at it from Jordan's side. Being given feedback, even well-structured feedback, often triggers a defensive reflex, and there are three common ones. Deny it: that's not what happened. Counter it: well, you missed one too. Or collapse: I'm useless at this. Each is understandable, and each ends the conversation before anything useful is learned. Denying and countering turn feedback into an argument; collapsing turns it into reassurance, so the person giving feedback ends up comforting the person receiving it. The alternative is to understand the feedback first, and decide what to do with it later. Pause before replying; a single breath is enough. Ask for a specific example: which handover was it? Ask what would have helped: what should I have done when I got pulled away? And thank the person for raising it, because raising it was probably not easy. None of this means accepting everything. You can disagree, but disagreement is more useful once you understand what was meant, and it often goes better after a day. Next, turning feedback into a step.

A feedback conversation that ends with I'll try harder usually changes nothing. A good one ends with something practical that both people agree to, and a time to check how it is going. Sam and Jordan agreed four things. Jordan will post a one-line note whenever pulled away from planned work. Alex will name a backup for handovers this week, which needs Alex's agreement, so Sam asks. Both will keep handover notes in the shared document, not in chat. And they will check in after two weeks. The check-in matters as much as the agreement. Two weeks later, the notes have worked: Jordan was pulled away twice and posted a note each time, and nobody was left waiting. One part needs adjusting: the backup was named but never briefed, so the backup would not have known what to hand over. That gets fixed. And Sam notices the change out loud, telling Jordan that the notes made a real difference. Feedback that is followed up, and change that is noticed, is how a single conversation becomes a lasting habit. Then the topic can be closed, or checked once more. Next, harder cases.

Two harder cases to finish. The first is feedback that is inaccurate. Priya, frustrated, says: your team never tells me anything. That is not true: updates go out every Tuesday. But it is clearly Priya's experience. Sam can separate the two. Acknowledge the impact: it sounds like you're not getting what you need. State the facts calmly: updates go out on Tuesdays, in the shared document. And propose a fix: would an email summary work better for you? It turns out Priya never opens the document. You can acknowledge someone's experience without accepting a claim that is false, and correcting it calmly is part of respecting them. The second case is power. Priya is the sponsor, so Sam is giving feedback upward. Upward feedback goes better when you ask first and tie it to a goal you share, such as a successful launch. Downward, people with more power need to invite challenge often and mean it, because others will rarely offer it unasked. Appreciation follows the same rules: specific, and timely. And if speaking up feels unsafe, that is not a feedback skill problem; other routes exist, which chapter nine covers. Next chapter: conflict.

Chapter nine is about conflict: disagreements where people want different things, and feelings run higher. The first step is to notice what kind of disagreement it is, because each kind needs a different response. Here is the argument. Priya wants the dashboard to launch on the fifteenth. Jordan wants three more weeks. That is a task disagreement, about what to do, and it is helped by evidence and options. But there is a process disagreement too: nobody is sure who actually decides the launch date. That is helped by clear decision rights, not by more debate. And there is the start of a relationship disagreement, when Priya says to Alex that Jordan always blocks things. That needs a private conversation, not a meeting. Real conflicts tend to drift through these kinds. They start as task disagreements about risk. Unclear process turns them into power struggles. And then they turn personal, with words like always and never, and guesses about motives. So the first move is to untangle it: which kind of disagreement is this, right now, and what does that kind need? Next, preparing for the conversation.

Jordan decides to talk to Priya directly, and takes ten minutes to prepare first. Preparation for a difficult conversation has five parts. The facts: three of the forty shops do not reconcile yet. Not the numbers are wrong, which is vaguer and more alarming, but exactly what is known. Jordan's own interests: numbers Jordan can stand behind. Priya's interests, as Jordan's best guess, which is labelled as a guess, to be checked in the conversation, not assumed. Jordan's limits: Jordan will not sign off totals that have not been checked. A limit is not a demand; it is the line Jordan will not cross, stated in advance so it is not invented in the heat of the moment. And the aim of the conversation itself. Not to win the argument. Not even to settle the date, which may be someone else's decision. The aim is for both people to leave with options they both understand. Writing the preparation down has another benefit: when the conversation gets tense, it steadies you, because you can look at what you decided you cared about when you were calm. Next, opening the conversation.

The first sentence of a difficult conversation often decides how the rest of it goes. Jordan could open with an accusation: your date is unrealistic. That may even be true, but Priya will hear an attack, and spend the conversation defending the date. Or Jordan could open with a shared aim: I want a launch plan that we can both trust; can I share a concern? That invites Priya in. In this case, Priya explains why the fifteenth matters: there is a demonstration for a key customer whose contract is up for renewal. Now Jordan's concern can be heard as a concern about that demonstration going well, not as an attack on Priya. Listening under tension is harder than listening in a calm meeting, and a few habits help. Summarise the other person's view before stating your own; it shows you heard it, and it often lowers the temperature. Notice the tension rising in yourself, and slow down. If it gets too hot, name a pause: can we take five minutes? And stay specific: this date, this risk, not always or never. Next, what sits underneath each side.

Underneath most conflicts are two layers. A position is what someone asks for. An interest is the reason they ask for it. Priya's position is a launch on the fifteenth. Jordan's position is a launch in three weeks. As positions, they are directly opposed: only one of them can win, and the conversation becomes a contest. But look at the interests. Priya needs a demonstration for a key customer whose contract renews soon, and needs to keep credibility with the director who promised it. Jordan needs numbers that reconcile, does not want to be blamed for errors in front of a customer, and would rather not spend the weekend firefighting. And now something appears that the positions hid: they share an interest. Both of them care about customer trust, and both want a launch that lands, not a launch followed by a recall. Positions often clash when interests do not. A simple question helps move from one to the other: what would that give you? Asked genuinely, and listened to, it usually reveals the interest. Next, building options from those interests.

Once both sets of interests are on the table, Priya and Jordan can look for options that meet both, and agree how to judge them before arguing about which one is best. They agree three criteria first. Demo: the customer sees real value on the fifteenth. Accuracy: only numbers that reconcile are shown. Load: the team does not work the weekend. Agreeing criteria first matters, because once options are on the table, people tend to choose the criteria that favour the option they already prefer. Then the options. A full launch on the fifteenth meets the demo criterion but fails accuracy and load. A launch in three weeks meets accuracy and load, but fails the demo. A third option appears from the interests: a limited demonstration on the fifteenth, using the thirty-seven shops whose numbers already reconcile, followed by the full release in three weeks. It meets all three criteria. It is not perfect, and the remaining risk stays visible: three shops are still unchecked, and the demo must not imply otherwise. But it is an option neither position would have produced. Next, what happens if they cannot agree.

What if Priya and Jordan cannot agree? Before agreeing to anything, it helps to know your best alternative if there is no agreement. Harvard's Program on Negotiation calls this a BATNA, a best alternative to a negotiated agreement. It is a reality check, not a threat to wave at the other person. Priya's realistic alternative is to show the old report at the demonstration, which looks dated. Jordan's is to flag the risk in writing, which adds tension and fixes nothing. And for both, the alternative is that Alex decides for them, and neither of them shapes the result. Compared honestly with these, the limited demonstration is better for both of them, which is a good sign that it is worth agreeing to. Authority limits matter here too. Neither Priya nor Jordan can set the launch date alone; Alex and the director can. And neither can promise anything on behalf of finance or the support team. So the agreement goes to Alex for approval, and it is recorded: what was agreed, who approved it, which risks are still open, and when to check that it is on track. Next, when a conversation is not the right route at all.

Most disagreements can be worked through with the approaches in this chapter. Some cannot, and some should not be. It is important to tell them apart. An ordinary disagreement, like the launch date, is best handled by a direct conversation. If people are stuck after genuinely trying, the next step is the manager, or a neutral facilitator who can help both sides be heard. Repeated personal attacks are not a disagreement to negotiate; they belong with the manager or with human resources. Harassment, discrimination, and retaliation against someone for raising a concern are different again. They are not matters for direct negotiation at all, because the harm is not something to trade off against anything else, and they belong in an organisation's formal reporting routes. And anything involving immediate danger goes to emergency services or security, straight away. A few things hold in all of these. Pausing a conversation is always allowed. Writing down what happened, with dates, the words used and any witnesses, helps later. Getting support from someone you trust matters. And organisations' policies differ, so it is worth finding yours before you need it. Next chapter: presenting.

Sam has ten minutes at the Thursday demo. The easiest talk to prepare is a tour: here is the overview tab, here is the shops tab, here are the filters, any questions? It feels thorough, but it leaves the work of deciding what matters to the audience. So Sam starts somewhere else: who is in the room, and what do they need to do? The director decides whether the dashboard rolls out to every shop. Priya needs a demo the customer will trust. Alex needs something the team can support at eight in the morning. Each of them needs a different part of the same story. From there Sam writes the central message as one sentence: the dashboard can replace the weekly spreadsheet, and we recommend rolling it out in three weeks. Everything else in the talk serves that sentence. The evidence that the numbers match finance. The limits: three shops still unchecked, data as of eleven. And the ask: a decision today. A useful test is whether you could say the message in a corridor. Next, the story behind it.

A project story becomes easy to follow when it has four parts. The context: the shops' sales were reported once a week, in a spreadsheet built by hand. The problem: it took about four hours a week, and the numbers were often a week old by the time anyone read them. The action: two daily loads, at six and eleven, showing only shops whose totals had been checked. The result: preparing the weekly numbers fell from four hours to twenty minutes over two weeks of use. That structure is a tool, and a story told well can still be untrue. So Sam checks each claim. Sam did not build the dashboard alone: Sam built the views, Jordan built the feed, and Mei found the refund bug before launch. Saying so costs nothing, and the people in the room may know anyway. The time saved was measured. Faster decisions are expected, but not yet measured, so Sam says expected. Storytelling organises what happened; it must not manufacture impact. Next, choosing the evidence and the visuals.

Sam has more evidence than ten minutes can hold, so Sam keeps only what supports the message. The comparison of dashboard totals with the finance ledger for the thirty-seven checked shops is the key claim, so it gets a chart. The time saved gets one number. The refund bug Mei found, and its fix, gets one honest line. Every other chart goes into an appendix for anyone who asks. Then the chart itself is annotated so it can be read correctly without Sam talking over it. The title states the finding: dashboard totals match finance within half a percent. The units: thousands of pounds of sales per day. The baseline: the finance ledger, for the same thirty-seven shops, so it is a like-for-like comparison. The axis starts at zero, so a small difference does not look like a large one. The limitation is on the chart, not hidden in speech: three shops are left out, and the data runs to eleven o'clock. And the source and dates. A limitation stated up front is far more credible than one discovered later by the audience. Next, rehearsal.

Sam rehearses the talk aloud, twice, with a timer. Reading slides silently is not rehearsal: the parts that are unclear, too long, or awkward to say only appear when you say them. The first run takes fourteen minutes, so two charts move to the appendix. Sam asks Mei to listen, with one question: where did you lose me? Mei is new, which makes Mei a good test: if the talk works for someone who joined a few weeks ago, it will work for the director. Sam keeps screenshots in case the live feed fails during the demo, and writes down the five questions most likely to come up, with a short answer to each. Nervousness is normal, and the aim is not to remove it. It peaks at the start, so Sam learns the first two sentences well. Pausing after each key number gives people time to read it, and gives Sam time to breathe. Notes on a card are fine. If Sam stumbles, the right move is to correct it and carry on; nobody needs an apology. Next, questions.

Halfway through, the director interrupts. Three shops are wrong, so why should anyone trust the rest? It is a fair question, and the tempting answers are all defensive. Dismissing it: those are basically fine. Guessing: it's probably a timing thing. Overpromising: it will be fixed by Monday. Each sounds confident in the moment and costs trust later, when the guess is wrong or Monday passes. Sam answers differently, in three parts. What is known: the thirty-seven checked shops match the finance ledger to within half a percent, over two weeks. What is unknown: why the other three differ. And the follow-up, with an owner and a date: Jordan will report the cause by Friday. That answer is honest about the gap, and it is more persuasive than confidence, because the director can check it. Not every interruption needs a full answer at once. If it would derail the talk, answer briefly or note it and come back to it at the end, and then do come back to it. Next, the close.

Sam's last minute is planned as carefully as the first. Ending with any questions, or that's about it, leaves the room without a decision, and then everyone remembers the demo but nobody knows what happens next. So Sam closes on four things. The recommendation: roll the dashboard out to every shop in three weeks. The decision needed: yes or no, today. The condition that makes it safe: run it alongside the spreadsheet for two weeks before the spreadsheet is retired. And the next step with an owner: Jordan reports on the three unreconciled shops by Friday. Then Sam takes questions, and after them restates the ask, because the questions can bury it. The same day, Sam sends a short written summary, so the decision and the owners are on record and not only in people's memories. The director approves the rollout, with the condition. That decision was not Sam's to make, and Sam did not need to make it. The next chapter is about exactly that: leading and influencing where you have no formal authority.

After the rollout, nobody on the team gains a new title, but plenty of leading still happens. Sam notices that shop managers keep asking for afternoon numbers, which the dashboard does not have. Jordan spends an hour pairing with Mei on the feed, so the knowledge does not sit with one person. Mei reports the refund bug without being asked to look for it. Alex names Jordan's work in the project review, so the credit lands where it belongs. And Jordan raised the launch-date risk early, when it was uncomfortable and still useful. Each of those is leadership: a behaviour, not a position. It is also easy to mistake for things it is not. Leading is not deciding on other people's behalf, being the loudest in the meeting, or taking every task yourself so nothing goes wrong. Those can look like leadership and often make the group weaker. The test is whether the behaviour serves the group's goal, or the leader's status. In this chapter, Sam turns the afternoon request into a proposal, without any authority over the people it affects. First: who it affects.

Sam's idea is a third daily load, at three in the afternoon, so shop managers can see the morning's sales before their four o'clock calls. Before proposing anything, Sam maps who the change touches. Priya wants the afternoon data and owns the budget that would pay for it. Jordan would build and maintain a third load on a feed that is already busy. Alex would need someone on support at three o'clock, every day. Each of those concerns is reasonable from where the person sits, and none of them is an obstacle to be got around. Then Sam separates the decisions, because they belong to different people. Whether the load is worth paying for is Priya's decision, as sponsor. How it is built is Jordan's, who owns the feed. Who supports it, and when, is Alex's, as support owner. Sam's own decision right is the smallest: whether to propose it at all. Anyone can propose; not everyone can decide. When decision rights are unclear, the useful move is to ask, before the proposal, not after it has been refused. Next, building support.

There are two ways Sam could introduce the three o'clock load. The fast way is to announce it: from Monday, we add a three o'clock load. It takes a minute. Jordan's first reaction is that nobody asked about the feed. Alex's is to ask who supports it at three. The proposal might be a good one, but now it arrives as something done to people, and it is resisted, then quietly dropped. The slower way starts by asking. Jordan says it is feasible if the afternoon load skips the refund recalculation, which can wait for the next morning. Alex says weekday support is fine, but weekends are not. Sam writes a short note with the evidence that shop managers ask for the data, the options, and both concerns stated in Jordan's and Alex's words, then takes it to Priya, who has the right to decide. Priya approves a one-month trial, on weekdays. Consulting took three days. It also produced a better design than Sam's original, and the people who will run it already agree with it. Next, coordinating the trial.

With the trial approved, Sam coordinates it. That role is real and useful, and it is not a management role. Sam can request: could you take the load job, Jordan? Sam can track owners and dates on one shared list, so nobody has to ask what is happening. Sam can remind people two days before a date, which helps, rather than the day after, which blames. And Sam can surface a problem early: telling Alex when a date is slipping, while there is still time to do something about it. What Sam cannot do is assign Jordan's time, which is Alex's decision; change another team's priorities; spend the trial budget, which is Priya's; or extend support to weekends, which Alex has already declined. Treating a coordination role as authority is a common way for good projects to create resentment. When a request is refused, the right move is to take the problem to someone who can decide: the date will slip unless someone frees two days of Jordan's time. That escalates the problem, not the person. Next, helping Mei grow.

Two weeks into the trial, the three o'clock load is slow, and Mei asks Sam: should I add an index, or rewrite the query? Sam could simply answer. Add an index on shop and date. It is fast and probably right, and next time Mei will ask again, because the answer was given but the reasoning was not. Mentoring aims at the second thing: Mei's own judgement. So Sam asks first. What did you measure? Mei has the timings for each step. What would each change fix? Mei thinks it through aloud. Which would you try first, and why? Mei says the index, because it is cheaper to undo, and then measure again. Only then does Sam give advice, and as advice: agreed, and check the query plan too. Asking first is not withholding help. If Mei were stuck, or the load were failing in production, Sam would just say what to do. And Sam suggests Mei writes the finding up in the team's notes, so the knowledge is shared beyond one conversation. Next, influence that stays honest.

The trial was Sam's idea, and it would be easy to push it harder than the evidence allows. A useful test for ethical influence: could the people being persuaded see everything you did, and still agree? Showing the weekend gap passes that test. Leaving it out of the note does not. A real deadline, such as the budget review, passes. An invented today-only urgency does not. Crediting Jordan and Mei passes; calling it my trial does not. Asking for objections passes; going around Jordan to Priya because Jordan objected does not. Jordan does still disagree: Jordan thinks the afternoon load is not worth its maintenance. Jordan says so, the concern goes into the note in Jordan's words, and then Jordan builds it properly anyway. Dissent was heard, and it did not need to win to be valuable. Follow-through is the last part of influence. The trial has a review date and a measure: whether the afternoon data is actually used. If it is not, Sam says so. The final chapter looks at what happens when conditions change.

A month after the three o'clock trial starts, Sam has the number: four of the forty shop managers used the afternoon data. It is disappointing, and the trial was Sam's idea, which makes it harder. The useful response is the same as for any other result. Sam reports it plainly, recommends ending the trial, and names the lesson: next time, ask the people who would use the data before building it. A setback reported early costs far less than one defended for months. At the same time, other things change, with incomplete information. Twelve new shops are joining, from a system nobody on the team has seen. Rather than plan for every possible format, Sam asks for one sample file, a small step that turns an unknown into something concrete. Alex is on leave for two weeks, so the team writes down who decides what while Alex is away. The four managers who did use the afternoon load hear it is ending before it is switched off. And the new finance system next year is noted, without a plan yet, because there is not enough to plan with. Next, learning from feedback.

Over the project, Sam has received a lot of feedback, and most of it is about one thing at a time. Looking across it, a pattern appears. Priya said a status update buried the ask. Alex said the demo was strong once Sam got to the decision. Mei said the first minute was hard to follow. Three different people, three different situations, one pattern: Sam starts with the detail and arrives at the point late. A single comment might be about one bad day. A pattern is worth acting on. Sam writes a short improvement note with three parts. One behaviour: open with the point or the ask. One regular opportunity to practise it: the Monday status note, every week. And, optionally, feedback: Sam might ask Alex in four weeks whether the updates are easier to read. It is deliberately small. A list of ten development goals gets read once; one behaviour practised every Monday changes how Sam writes. The note is for Sam, not a formal assessment, and stays private unless Sam chooses to share it. Next, relationships and asking for help.

Sam wants to get better at presenting to senior people, and a senior analyst in another team does it well. The vague way to ask is: will you be my mentor? Or: can I pick your brain sometime? Both ask for open-ended time, for an unclear purpose, and they are hard to say yes to and awkward to refuse. A focused request is different. It gives context: I present to directors in March. It asks for something specific and small: could I have thirty minutes on how you open a presentation? It makes no easy to say: no problem if it is a busy month. And it gives something back. Sam offers to share the notes from the conversation, and later tells the analyst how the presentation went, which most people who give advice never hear. Many lasting mentoring relationships start this way: one useful conversation, followed by another. Networking works the same way. It is not collecting contacts; it is being useful to people over time, including helping others, like Mei, who are earlier in their careers. Next, explaining your contributions.

A year later, Sam is in an interview, and the question is: tell me about something you did that didn't work. Sam has the answer ready, organised as situation, task, action and result. The situation: shop managers asked for afternoon data. The task: it was Sam's proposal, and Sam coordinated it. The action: Sam consulted the feed owner and the support owner, and the sponsor approved a one-month trial. The result: four of forty managers used it, so the team ended it. And the part interviewers listen for most: what Sam learned, which is to ask the people who would use something before building it, and that Sam has done so since, with the new shops. The structure only helps if the story is accurate. Sam built the dashboard's views and the demo, so Sam says that, not I led the dashboard. Sam uses I for Sam's own part and names the others. An honest unsuccessful outcome answers the question that was actually asked, and it is far more convincing than a failure that turns out to be a success in disguise. Next, the whole project together.

Seen end to end, the dashboard project is a chain of ordinary moments. At the brief, Priya asked for real time, and clarifying questions found that two loads a day, at six and eleven, met the actual need. When the eleven o'clock load ran three hours late, an early, plain update meant the Thursday demo went ahead with an as-of-eleven note instead of a surprise. When scope and time collided, the plan traded columns for the date: six columns, a manual file on Monday, the export on Wednesday. When Priya and Jordan disagreed about the launch, looking at interests and agreed criteria produced a limited demo of thirty-seven checked shops and a full release in three weeks. The presentation ended on a clear ask, and the rollout was approved with a condition. And the review reported the three o'clock trial as the setback it was. None of these was dramatic. Each one made the next conversation easier. Some things remain uncertain: whether the shops will still use the dashboard in six months, and what the twelve new shops' data looks like. Good practice does not remove uncertainty; it surfaces it early. Next, sustaining it.

This course has described skills, and describing them is the easy part. They grow through practice in real conversations, a little reflection, and honest feedback over time. A sustainable routine is small. Fifteen minutes on a Friday to note what happened that week and what to repeat. One behaviour at a time, practised somewhere that happens every week. People: a mentor, peers, and someone who will tell you honestly how it went. And rest, because a team that fights fires every weekend has a planning problem, not a resilience problem. That points to the limit of everything in this course. Some problems are not personal skill gaps. Overtime every week, or targets nobody can meet, are worth raising with your manager, with evidence. Unsafe conditions, discrimination and harassment go through formal routes, not better conversations. Communication habits do not fix an unsafe or unfair workplace, and you should not be asked to absorb one. Workplace relationships and lasting behaviour change take experience beyond any course. The next step is the next ordinary conversation, and paying attention to what actually happens.
